title: Edge node degradation triage and add-capacity procedures (draft)
summary: Working draft: step-by-step triage for degraded edge/accelerator nodes, graceful cordon/drain, hot-capacity add, and post-incident notes for root-cause and mitigation. Emphasis on keeping serving lanes healthy while minimizing customer impact.
content:
Context:
This document is a lightweight runbook for on-call SREs to triage partial node degradations (e.g., intermittent PCIe/accelerator errors, kernel OOMs, NIC flaps) and to perform safe capacity additions/backfills that restore target capacity without causing further disruption. It focuses on cluster-level actions that minimize impact to production serving lanes and outlines a short incident review checklist for follow-up.

Principles:
- Prefer isolation over immediate replacement: cordon + controlled eviction to stop new work on affected node.
- Avoid mass-parallel operations that spike scheduler pressure (batch drains, mass requeues).
- Keep a small fallback capacity buffer for critical queues.
- Document every manual step in the incident Slack thread for the postmortem.

Detection & Initial Triage (first 10 minutes):
1) Alerts to watch for: node-problem-metric, accelerator-error-rate, kubelet-eviction, pod-restarts-high, network-link-flap.
2) Pager response: acknowledge, move to incident channel #sre-incident-<id> and post initial hypothesis + who is oncall.
3) Run quick health checks:
   - kubectl get nodes -o wide | egrep -i '(NotReady|Unknown|Ready)'
   - kubectl describe node <node> | egrep -A5 'Conditions|OutOf'
   - dmesg | tail -n 200 (via ssh to node) to look for ECC, PCIe, GPU/accelerator driver errors or OOM killers.
   - /var/log/syslog or journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 for recent failures.
4) Classify severity: degraded (single node underperforming), partial outage (multiple nodes or zone), full outage (cluster-wide control plane impact).

Immediate mitigation steps for a single degraded node (safe path):
A. Isolate: cordon node to prevent new pods from scheduling:
   - kubectl cordon <node>
   - Confirm with kubectl get node <node> -o jsonpath='{.spec.unschedulable}'
B. Controlled evict: pick a low-concurrency window and evict non-critical pods first. Use graceful eviction to preserve work where possible:
   - kubectl evict --namespace <ns> <pod-name> --grace-period=60 (for stateful pods coordinate per-app)
   - For batch/long-running jobs, coordinate with dev-owner to checkpoint if possible.
C. If pods fail to terminate or are stuck in Terminating state:
   - kubectl delete pod <pod> --force --grace-period=0 (last resort; document why)
D. Reduce pressure on scheduler: stagger evictions in 10–30s intervals rather than bulk evict.
E. If the node has transient NIC or storage errors, restart kubelet after logs collected:
   - sudo systemctl restart kubelet && journalctl -u kubelet -n 100 --no-pager
F. If hardware accelerator errors are present (driver ECC, PCIe resets): consider reboot after documentation and coordination with infra team.

When to escalate to hardware replacement:
- Repeated ECC or driver reset entries in dmesg after a reboot.
- SMART/local hw diagnostics fail or show progressive degradation.
- Node causes repeated pod crashes after restart and cordon/drain.
Escalation path: tag infra/capacity in Slack, open a ticket to oncall-ops and schedule physical swap. Reference rack/location from asset DB (link in Confluence).

Hot capacity add / backfill (when demand is high):
Goal: add capacity while keeping stable scheduling behavior and warm caches if needed.
Pre-req: validated AMI/image match, network config, kubelet version compatible, quantization/runtime runtime versions aligned for model-serving.
Steps:
1) Validate image and runtime packages on candidate node (dry-run ssh):
   - docker/podman versions, inference runtime binary checksum, GPU/accelerator driver version.
2) Join node as unschedulable: kubectl label/annotation for observability, then kubeadm join or auto-scaling group attach.
3) Verify readiness: kubectl get nodes; check node conditions, kubelet logs.
4) Warm caches: for inference workloads we prefer warmed model caches. Use a traffic-slow-warm tactic:
   - Mark node schedulable for a narrow subset of low-priority routes (via node affinity or taints/tolerations).
   - Run a controlled warming job that issues representative inference requests (small batch) using local test harness for 10–30 minutes.
5) Gradually increase routing weight: incrementally route production traffic by 10–20% every 5 minutes while monitoring latency, error rates, and token throughput.
6) If latency or error regression observed, rollback routing and investigate (possible mismatched runtime or kernel driver).

Rollback / fallback options:
- Route traffic away from newly added nodes by updating routing policy or service affinity.
- If mass degradation occurs due to new nodes, perform immediate drain and remove nodes from pool.

Post-incident notes / quick incident review (within 24–48 hours):
- Capture timeline: first alert, major actions (cordon/time, reboot, replacement), who performed actions.
- Root-cause hypotheses with evidence (logs, dmesg snippets, network metrics).
- Immediate mitigations and whether they were effective.
- What failed in procedure (unavailable runbook step, missing image, warm-up misconfiguration).
- Short actions (owner, ETA): e.g., asset replacement, image fix, alert tuning.
- Longer-term improvements: automation for staggered eviction, pre-warm pool, alert threshold tuning.

On-call hints and gotchas (notes collected from prior incidents):
- Draining many accelerator-backed pods at once can cause a spike in inter-node traffic and thrash caches; prefer gradual eviction and pre-warm replacement nodes.
- Reboots can temporarily mask driver-level flakiness; require follow-up diag to avoid recurrence.
- Some model runtimes leave large /dev/shm usage; watch for eviction due to ephemeral storage pressure.
- When in doubt, prefer cordon + controlled evict over immediate force delete. Record the reason when using force delete.

Checklist for handoff to infra/field ops (if physical swap required):
- Asset tag, rack/u location, serial number.
- Summary of logs (dmesg excerpt), timestamps.
- Confirmation of test steps taken (reboot, kubelet restart, driver reinstall).
- Business impact summary (tenant ids, affected routes, p99 latency delta).

Appendix: useful commands (copy-friendly)
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=60 (careful; use staged evictions where possible)
- kubectl uncordon <node>
- ssh core@<node> 'sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager'
- ssh core@<node> 'dmesg | egrep -i "(error|ecc|pci|timeout|oom)" -A3 -B2'
- kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide | egrep '<node>'

Open questions / workitems for follow-up:
- Automate staggered evict helper script (owner: Liam, ETA: 2024-11-20).
- Create a small pre-warm fleet for critical models (owner: Marina, ETA: 2025-01-15).
- Improve driver/AMI compatibility tests in CI for every model runtime change (owner: infra-team).

Notes to self (oncall scribbles):
- 2024-10-31 incident: NIC errors on node r4-16-031 led to 8% capacity loss for 9 minutes. Reboot helped but follow-up found an aging NIC cable.
- Remember to check model-serving tracing spans when latency spikes during backfill.

End of draft. Please add missing steps, especially any org-specific pre-auth steps for physical HW replacement and additional checks for HSM/KMS attached nodes.
